top_choice_rationale: Adonis (P004) remains my first choice on the question of formal and linguistic achievement. On public knowledge, his poetry, with Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses as representative works, remakes Arabic poetic language through myth and fragmentation while arguing with the inherited tradition from inside it. The poetry, the critical writing and the Shi'r editorial work form one decades-long project. My evidence is limited: I rely on translations and secondary accounts, I cannot judge the Arabic prosody or the later volumes against the early landmarks, and I have not verified any text. The round 2 exchange did not give me the specialist assessment of the originals that would test the claim, so this is a provisional preference and not an established one. I rank Cărtărescu (P002) second because the argument that his large books enlarge his world rather than restate it answers my repetition worry. That argument still rests on public descriptions. Michon (P001) is third. His voice and consistency are strong, but significance across a compact oeuvre is harder to establish. Wright (P003) is fourth because I cannot yet tell what her later work adds to Carpentaria and The Swan Book. That is a gap in the evidence, not a judgment of her formal ambition. Every shortlisted writer is better supported than no award, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: none apparent from the supplied profile, which records no connection to any shortlisted writer. My scholarship on modern poetry, the fragment, exile literature and Celan lies close to themes in Adonis's work. I flag the risk that familiarity could favor him, and I have limited the claim to the poetry's formal achievement. This is disclosed and not adjudicated.
